title: In Vivo Three-Photon Microscopy Analysis of B Lineage Cell Dynamics in Mouse Tibia
author: Bias, Fiedler, et al.
materials:
Timing: 30–45 min
9.Mouse anesthesia.a.Holding the mouse (CD19:tdRFP fate mapping mouse strain) fixed, apply an inhalation mask on its nose.Note: For ventilation, use a mixture of oxygen and isoflurane (isoflurane concentration between 1.5 and 2%).b.Adjust the concentration of isoflurane and oxygen flow rate according to the weight of the mouse.Note: For a mouse mass between 20 g and 35 g, use flow rates between 200 mL/min and 500 mL/min.10.Place the anesthetized mouse on a heated plate and keep the core temperature at 37°C, e.g. using a rectal thermometer.11.Mouse surgery for imaging.a.Fix the right hind paw by stretching the leg to the side.b.To prevent contamination, shave the fur over the entire limb.c.Make an incision in the skin above the tibia.d.Push the tibialis anterior muscle aside, to expose the flat medial surface of the tibia shaft.e.To keep the tibia in position, fix the crest with a surgical hook.Figure 4Three-photon imaging at 1650 nm (3 MHz repetition rate) in intact tibia of CD19:LSL-tdRFP mice(A) Picture of the mouse leg showing the tibia prepared for imaging, with the search area marked by the gray dashed line.(B) Rendering of an overview 3D image in the mouse tibia of a CD19:LSL-tdRFP mouse, used for orientation in tissue. Third harmonics generation (THG, green) and tdRFP fluorescence signal (magenta) in marrow (C) lineage cells allow to differentiate between bone cortex and bone marrow. Yellow dashed box indicates the volume defined for time-lapse imaging. (B) Rendering of the 3D volume (400 × 400 × 30 μm3) imaged in a time-lapse manner (time step = 30 s). Scale bar: 50 μm.

12.Preparation of the imaging site for using the water immersion objective lens.a.Build a low melting agarose wall (1% agarose) around the open area to form a cylindrical bath.b.Fill the agarose cone with isotonic NaCl solution as immersion medium for imaging.c.Fill up the still fluid agarose in a syringe (without a needle) to build the agarose wall layer by layer.

steps.title: Anesthetize mouse
steps.instruction: Place the CD19:tdRFP mouse under an inhalation mask, deliver a mixture of oxygen and isoflurane (1.5–2% isoflurane) and adjust the oxygen flow to 200–500 mL min⁻¹ according to the mouse weight (20–35 g).

steps.title: Maintain core temperature
steps.instruction: Transfer the anesthetized mouse onto a heated plate and keep the core temperature at 37 °C (monitor with a rectal thermometer).

steps.title: Prepare tibia for imaging
steps.instruction: Fix the right hind paw by stretching the leg laterally, shave the entire limb, make a skin incision above the tibia, push the tibialis anterior muscle aside to expose the flat medial surface, and secure the tibial crest with a surgical hook.

steps.title: Create agarose imaging bath
steps.instruction: Form a cylindrical wall of 1 % low‑melting agarose around the exposed tibia, fill the agarose cone with isotonic NaCl solution, and build the wall layer‑by‑layer by injecting agarose from a syringe without a needle.

steps.title: Acquire three‑photon data
steps.instruction: Using the 1650 nm optical parametric amplifier (3 MHz repetition rate), image the intact tibia marrow through the agarose bath, acquiring a 3‑D volume of 400 × 400 × 30 µm³ with a time step of 30 s; the searchable imaging area is ~10 mm² on the anterior tibia.

steps.title: Train Noise2Void model
steps.instruction: In FIJI/CSBDeep, train the Noise2Void (N2V) deep‑learning plug‑in on high‑SNR 3‑D stacks of B‑cell fluorescence (or on 2‑D data for comparison) using 20 images per run, 200 epochs, 300 steps per epoch, batch size 128–256, and a neighborhood radius of 5.

steps.title: Validate denoising model
steps.instruction: Apply the trained N2V model to independent high‑SNR data (not used for training) and to low‑SNR data obtained through intact bone to confirm improved SNR (e.g., from 1.8 dB to >5 dB).

steps.title: Denoise time‑lapse data
steps.instruction: Run the validated N2V model on the acquired time‑lapse 3‑D stacks to reduce pixel‑wise noise before segmentation and tracking.

steps.title: Load data into Imaris
steps.instruction: Import the denoised 3‑D time‑lapse series into Imaris and set the spatial dimensions (µm) and time dimension (seconds) to match the acquisition parameters.

steps.title: Segment and track cells
steps.instruction: Create a Surface object with surface roughness = 1 µm, use local contrast Watershed (largest sphere = 7 µm), split objects with an average size of 10 µm, exclude objects < 65 µm³ (≈20 µm diameter), then track using Autoregressive Motion (max step distance = 15 µm, max gap = 1). Visually inspect tracks and manually merge or split erroneous tracks.

steps.title: Classify B vs plasma cells
steps.instruction: In the Surface environment, define two groups by volume: B cells (65–500 µm³) and plasma cells (500–4100 µm³).

steps.title: Export trajectory statistics
steps.instruction: Extract per‑cell trajectories, displacements, track lengths and durations and save them as CSV or TXT files.

steps.title: Generate rose plots
steps.instruction: Run the provided Python script (matplotlib, mpl_toolkits.mplot3d, numpy) on the exported trajectory file to produce 3‑D rose plots (axes –50 to +50 µm).

steps.title: Statistical analysis of motility
steps.instruction: Import displacement, track length and duration files into Origin (or Excel/Python/Matlab), compute average velocity (track length ÷ duration) and displacement rate (displacement ÷ duration), and perform statistical comparisons between B cells and plasma cells.

description: Three-photon microscopy (3PM) allows in vivo deep-tissue imaging of optically hardly accessible organs, beyond the capabilities of two-photon microscopy (2PM) due to long wavelength excitation, either in NIR I (1300 nm) or NIR II (1700 nm) tissue windows.2,3,4 Several improvements of the optical system, including beam shaping,5 adaptive optics,6,7,8,9,10,11 the design of new objective lens concepts,12 as well as the development of dedicated fluorophores are currently boosting the application of the technology.13 3PM performance has been successfully demonstrated in vivo in brain cortex,6,14,15 deep tumor16 as well as soft lymphoid organs imaging.17 Due to strong scattering effects in calcified bone, perturbation-free in vivo imaging of the marrow cavity through the intact thick bone cortex in long bones of adult mice still poses a challenge. This strong scattering is related to the fact that bone has the highest refractive index span among mammalian tissues (from n ≈1.33 up to ≈1.62),18,19,20 for comparison, the refractive index of soft lymphoid tissues ranges between ≈1.33 and ≈1.4.18,21 The importance of bone marrow imaging can hardly be overestimated: as primary lymphoid tissue, the bone marrow is the birthplace of most immune cells,22 including B cells, and the final destination of terminally differentiated cells ensuring long-term immunological memory, such as plasma cells.23 We previously described the implementation of an optical parametric amplifier prototype emitting at 1650 nm with a variable repetition rate between 1 and 4 MHz in 3PM and demonstrated its performance for in vivo imaging of the tibia marrow through the intact bone cortex in mice.1 In this way, we were able to perform time-lapse imaging over large imaging volumes (400 × 400 × 30 μm3) in CD19:LSL-tdRFP fate mapping mice and to analyze the dynamics of B lymphocytes, without inducing tissue photo damage.
